0.title: The Architecture of Redemption
0.overview:
Covenant theology is not a theological option for the academically inclined. It is the framework within which the whole Bible makes sense. Without it, Scripture becomes a collection of disconnected stories — inspiring, perhaps, but ultimately lacking the inner logic that binds Genesis to Revelation into a single, unified, coherent narrative. With it, every part of the Bible finds its place in a sweeping, God-directed drama whose theme is one: the triune God binding Himself, by oath and blood, to a people He has chosen, redeemed, and is bringing home.

A covenant, in the biblical world, is not merely a contract or an agreement between equals. It is a solemn, oath-bound relationship, typically sealed with a sacrifice (the animals cut in pieces, the blood shed), that creates a bond of loyalty, obligation, and belonging between the parties. When God condescends to enter into covenant with His creatures, He is doing something of staggering condescension: the infinite, self-sufficient, all-glorious God binding Himself — by His own oath, on His own initiative, at His own cost — to be the God of His people. "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" is the covenant formula, and it echoes from Eden to the New Jerusalem.

This study traces the great covenants of Scripture: the eternal Covenant of Redemption within the Trinity, the Covenant of Works with Adam, and the Covenant of Grace that runs from the promise of Genesis 3:15 through Noah, Abraham, Moses, and David to its culmination in the new covenant of Jesus Christ. Along the way we ask how these covenants relate to each other, what covenant theology means for how we read the Old Testament, and what it means for the disputed question of baptism.
0.theology:
Covenant as Structural Principle

Reformed biblical theology has always insisted that covenant is not merely one theme among many in Scripture — it is the structural principle of the whole. The Westminster Confession of Faith (Chapter 7) introduces the doctrine of the covenant as God's gracious condescension to creatures who could never put God under obligation: "The distance between God and the creature is so great, that although reasonable creatures do owe obedience unto him as their Creator, yet they could never have any fruition of him as their blessedness and reward, but by some voluntary condescension on God's part, which he hath been pleased to express by way of covenant."

The Unity of the Two Testaments

Covenant theology is the Reformed answer to the question: How does the Old Testament relate to the New? The answer is: as promise to fulfilment, as shadow to substance, as type to antitype — but within the framework of one overarching Covenant of Grace, administered differently across the ages but never replaced or abandoned. This is what allows the Reformed tradition to read the Old Testament as Christian Scripture: its covenants, ceremonies, and prophecies all point forward to Christ, in whom they find their "yes and amen" (2 Cor 1:20).

Sources

This study draws on Herman Witsius (The Economy of the Covenants), John Murray (The Covenant of Grace), O. Palmer Robertson (The Christ of the Covenants), Michael Horton (God of Promise), Geerhardus Vos, and the Westminster Standards — alongside Calvin, Owen, and contemporary voices including Sinclair Ferguson and Ligon Duncan.
0.examples:
Then: The Reformation recovered justification by faith; the post-Reformation Reformed tradition developed covenant theology as the biblical-theological framework within which justification makes sense. The great federal theologians of the seventeenth century — Johannes Cocceius, Herman Witsius, Francis Turretin — showed that Scripture's narrative is not a random sequence of dispensations but a single, progressive, covenant-structured drama. The Westminster Assembly embedded this framework in the Confession (chapters 7–8) and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, making covenant theology the backbone of the Presbyterian and Reformed tradition.

Now: Dispensationalism — which divides Scripture into distinct epochs governed by different principles — remains the dominant framework in much of popular evangelicalism. Covenant theology offers a more unified, Christ-centred reading of Scripture, in which every covenant finds its fulfilment in Christ, the Old Testament is read as genuine Christian Scripture (not a historical prelude to the real story), and the people of God across all ages are understood as one people, saved by one grace, through one faith in one Mediator. Understanding this framework does not merely settle academic debates — it transforms how you read your Bible, how you pray, how you understand the church, and how you raise your children.

1.title: The Covenant of Redemption
1.overview:
Before the world was made, before Adam drew breath, before sin entered and ruined everything, a covenant was struck. Not between God and humanity, but within the Godhead itself — between the Father and the Son, in the Spirit, an eternal agreement in which the Son volunteered to enter the human story as the last Adam, to take on human nature, to live the life of perfect obedience that humanity owed and could not render, and to bear the penalty for sins that were not His own. This eternal, intra-Trinitarian covenant is called the pactum salutis — the covenant of redemption — and it is the ultimate ground of all salvation.

This is not a speculative doctrine invented by scholastic theologians to fill empty hours. It is rooted in the texture of Scripture itself: in passages where the Father addresses the Son about a people given to Him before the world began (John 6:37–40; 17:2, 6, 9, 24), where the Son comes not to do His own will but the will of the One who sent Him (John 6:38; Heb 10:5–10), where the Spirit is promised as the gift the exalted Christ will pour out on His redeemed people (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; Acts 2:33). The salvation of sinners is not an afterthought improvised in response to the fall — it is an eternal purpose, established in the love of the Trinity before time began.

The pastoral significance is immense. When a believer trusts in Christ, they are not relying on a plan devised in haste or a promise made without full counting of the cost. They are the beneficiaries of an eternal covenant, ratified by the blood of the Son who agreed from eternity to be their surety. Their salvation is as old as God's love, as certain as the Son's faithfulness, and as invincible as the Father's purpose.
1.theology:
The Three Parties

The classical Reformed formulation identifies three parties in the covenant of redemption: the Father, who appoints the Son as Mediator and gives Him a people; the Son, who accepts the commission and pledges to accomplish the work of redemption; and the Holy Spirit, who is promised as the gift of the new covenant, through whom the Son's work is applied to the redeemed. The Trinity does not merely co-operate in salvation — the three Persons play distinct and irreplaceable roles, each flowing from the eternal covenant.

The Son as Surety

The key term in the pactum salutis is that the Son becomes the surety of the covenant people — the One who stands in their place, takes their obligations, and answers for their failures. Hebrews 7:22 is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus is explicitly called a "surety" (Greek enguos): "Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant." A surety is one who takes full legal responsibility for another's debt. The Son's eternal agreement to be humanity's surety is the foundation on which every other covenant is built.

Objections and Responses

Some object that a covenant requires two distinct parties, making an intra-Trinitarian covenant impossible. The Reformed response is that while the Persons of the Trinity share one divine essence, they are genuinely distinct — and Scripture presents the Father and Son in genuine covenantal dialogue (Ps 2:7–9; Ps 110:1; Isa 42:1–9; Zech 6:12–13; John 17). The language of "giving" and "receiving," of commission and obedience, of promise and fulfilment, is real language describing a real eternal relationship between distinct Persons.
1.examples:
Then: The doctrine of the pactum salutis was developed with great care by the post-Reformation Reformed scholastics, particularly Francis Turretin, Herman Witsius, and the Westminster Divines. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q.31) describes it as the Father's "free and special love" in choosing the elect and the Son's "voluntary undertaking" of their redemption. John Owen's Communion with God beautifully expounds the distinct roles of each Person of the Trinity in the work of salvation — a work rooted in the eternal counsel of the Triune God.

Now: The pastoral recovery of this doctrine addresses one of the deepest anxieties of the Christian life: Is my salvation secure? The answer covenant theology gives is: your salvation was secured before the world began, in the eternal purpose of the Father, the eternal pledge of the Son, and the eternal gift of the Spirit. You are not relying on a decision you made or a prayer you prayed; you are relying on an eternal covenant ratified in the blood of the Son who agreed from before creation to be your Saviour.

verseByVerse.ref: The Father Gives a People to the Son
verseByVerse.quote: All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me. — John 6:37–38
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus here speaks of a people the Father has given Him — a definite, particular company whose coming to the Son is both certain ("will come") and permanent ("I will never cast out"). The language of "giving" is covenantal: the Father has, in the eternal counsel, entrusted a people to the Son, and the Son's coming into the world is precisely to fulfill that covenantal commission. He comes "not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me" — the sending and the mandate belong to the covenant of redemption.

The security the passage offers is absolute: not one of those the Father has given will be lost (v.39). This is not merely a promise about the future; it is a statement about the reliability of an eternal covenant. The Son does not lose what the Father has given because His agreement to keep them is as eternal as the giving itself. Herman Witsius saw this passage as one of the clearest windows into the pactum salutis in all of Scripture: here is the Father's side (He gives a people) and the Son's side (He receives them and pledges to lose none) of an eternal covenant, disclosed within time for the comfort of believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, 'Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.' — Hebrews 10:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 40:6–8 and applies it to the incarnation of the Son. The "scroll of the book" in which the Son's mission is written is not a document drafted at Bethlehem — it is the eternal decree, the pactum salutis, in which the Son's coming and His mission were determined before time. "I have come to do your will" is the Son's expression, in time, of an eternal commitment: He has always been the One commissioned to accomplish redemption; the incarnation is the historical enactment of an eternal covenant.

The context in Hebrews 10 is the inadequacy of animal sacrifices: they could not take away sins (v.4), and they had to be repeated endlessly. The Son's coming replaces them with a single, sufficient, once-for-all obedience and sacrifice (vv.10, 14). This is the covenant of redemption meeting history: what was agreed in eternity is accomplished in time, by the Son who took on a body (v.5) in order to offer Himself. The obedience of the earthly ministry — from Bethlehem to Calvary — is the temporal expression of the eternal willingness captured in Psalm 40.

verseByVerse.ref: The Father's Promise to the Son
verseByVerse.quote: Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession. — Psalm 2:8
verseByVerse.commentary:
Psalm 2 is a royal psalm that the New Testament consistently reads as a dialogue between the Father and the Son (Acts 4:25–27; 13:33; Heb 1:5; 5:5). The Father addresses the Son: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you" (v.7). The Son is then invited to ask for His inheritance — the nations, the ends of the earth. This is the covenant of redemption in the Psalter: the Father promises the Son a universal inheritance, a redeemed people gathered from every corner of the earth, as the reward of His messianic work.

The promise grounds the Great Commission (Matt 28:18–20): the risen Christ commands His disciples to make disciples of all nations because He has been given all authority (v.18) — He is claiming His Psalm 2 inheritance. Mission is not a human program; it is the fulfilment of the Father's eternal promise to the Son. Every convert from every nation is the Son receiving what the Father promised Him before the world began. O. Palmer Robertson saw in this psalm the clearest Old Testament window into the Trinitarian covenant of redemption: two Persons, a commission, a promise, an eternal purpose being worked out in history.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth... — John 14:16–17
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Holy Spirit's coming at Pentecost is not a surprise addition to the plan of salvation — it is the fulfilment of a promise embedded in the covenant of redemption. The Son, having accomplished His work of obedience and sacrifice, asks the Father to send the Spirit, and the Father gives Him. The Spirit is the "another Helper" (Greek allos paraklētos — another of the same kind as the Son), the One through whom the Son's work is applied to the redeemed people the Father gave Him.

Acts 2:33 makes the covenantal structure explicit: "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing." The Spirit is the Father's promise to the Son, given as the Son's exaltation gift — and poured out by the Son on the people He has redeemed. Sinclair Ferguson's The Holy Spirit traces this covenantal logic with great care: the Spirit is not an afterthought or a supplement to the Son's work but the Third Person of the Trinity whose role in the pactum salutis is to apply to the elect what the Son accomplished for the elect.

2.title: The Covenant of Works
2.overview:
Adam stood in the garden not merely as a private individual but as a representative — a federal head, a covenant head — for the whole human race. The arrangement between God and Adam in Eden was covenantal: God placed Adam under a specific probationary command (not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil), with life promised for obedience and death threatened for disobedience. The principle operating in this arrangement was works: do this and live, fail and die. This is what the Reformed tradition calls the Covenant of Works.

This doctrine matters enormously, because it provides the framework for understanding both the fall and the redemption. If Adam was a private individual, his sin is his own affair and its consequences affect him alone. But if Adam was a covenant head — a representative whose standing before God was the standing of all those he represented — then when Adam fell, all fell; when Adam was condemned, all were condemned; when Adam's nature was corrupted, all inherited a corrupted nature. This is precisely Paul's argument in Romans 5:12–21: death spread to all because all sinned in Adam, and the comparison with Christ (the last Adam) only works if both are functioning as covenant representatives.

The covenant of works also explains why the gospel is structured as it is. If Adam failed the probation, and his failure is imputed to all his descendants, then what humanity needs is a new covenant head — a second Adam who will succeed where the first failed, whose obedience will be as real and as consequential as Adam's disobedience. This is exactly what Christ is and does. The covenant of works is not an obscure theological curiosity; it is the dark background against which the gospel blazes with its greatest brightness.
2.theology:
Federal Headship

The doctrine of federal headship — that Adam (and subsequently Christ) acted as a legal representative for others — is the key to understanding both the fall and redemption. The Westminster Confession (Chapter 7.2) states that God made a covenant with Adam "and in him with his posterity." This representative function is what allows Paul to say "in Adam all die" and "in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Cor 15:22). The two Adams are covenant heads; their acts have representative, imputed consequences for those they represent.

Was the Covenant of Works Gracious?

Some Reformed theologians have resisted calling the Eden arrangement a "covenant" because the word "covenant" does not appear in Genesis 2, and because the relationship between God and Adam was already one of grace (God condescending to create and bless). The majority Reformed position, however, maintains the distinction: while God's condescension to create Adam was itself an act of grace, the specific probationary arrangement in Eden operated on the principle of works — obedience yielding life, disobedience yielding death. This does not make the arrangement graceless; it makes it different in principle from the Covenant of Grace that follows.

Hosea 6:7

Hosea 6:7 — "But like Adam they transgressed the covenant" — is the clearest biblical indication that the Eden arrangement was a covenant in the formal sense. The comparison between Israel's covenant-breaking and Adam's covenant-breaking implies that Adam was indeed in a covenantal relationship with God, and that his transgression was a covenant violation with representative consequences.
2.examples:
Then: The Covenant of Works was articulated clearly by the Westminster Assembly and by federal theologians like Johannes Cocceius and Francis Turretin. It was the framework within which they understood original sin, the imputation of Adam's guilt, and the active obedience of Christ. The Larger Catechism (Q.20) states that "the covenant of works being broken by sin, and made unprofitable unto life, God was pleased to give forth the promise of Christ" — showing the direct connection between the broken covenant of works and the instituted covenant of grace.

Now: The doctrine is resisted today on multiple grounds: some find the idea of legal representation morally objectionable, others question whether a probationary arrangement with Adam can be found in the text of Genesis 2. But the cost of abandoning it is high: without federal headship in Adam, the parallel with federal headship in Christ (the backbone of Romans 5) loses its theological logic. To deny the Covenant of Works is ultimately to undermine the imputation of Christ's righteousness — which is the heart of justification.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, 'You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.' — Genesis 2:16–17
verseByVerse.commentary:
The structure of the Covenant of Works is laid out here with precision: a sovereign command, a prohibition, and a sanction (death for disobedience). What is absent from the text — and what the Westminster Divines inferred from the broader canonical witness — is an explicit statement of the positive reward. But the logic of the covenant implies it: the tree of life (2:9) represents the life that faithful obedience would have confirmed; Adam's expulsion from its presence (3:22–24) shows that access to it was the prize at stake. Reformed theologians from Calvin onward have read Genesis 2:16–17 as the legal core of the Edenic covenant: God as sovereign legislator, Adam as covenant servant, life and death as the covenant sanctions.

The lavishness of the positive grant is striking: "you may surely eat of every tree of the garden" — the abundance is staggering, the restriction minimal. One tree, one prohibition, against the backdrop of unimaginable generosity. The probation was not designed to be difficult; it was designed to be the setting in which Adam's loyalty to his Creator could be expressed and confirmed. The tragedy of the fall is not merely that Adam failed — it is that he failed so easily, so unnecessarily, with so much given and so little asked.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned... — Romans 5:12
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's argument in Romans 5:12–21 is the most extended and theologically precise treatment of federal headship in the New Testament. The logic moves from Adam's sin to universal death — and the reason death spread to all is "because all sinned." This is not a reference to personal sins (as if everyone who dies has personally sinned enough to deserve death) but to representative sin: all sinned in Adam, in the covenant head whose act counts for all those he represents.

The argument only reaches its goal in verse 18: "as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men." The parallelism is the whole point: Adam's one trespass, imputed to all he represented, is the mirror image of Christ's one act of righteousness, imputed to all He represents. If you deny the imputation of Adam's sin, you saw off the very branch on which the imputation of Christ's righteousness sits. John Murray's commentary on Romans 5 remains one of the finest treatments of this passage, showing with exegetical rigour how the Adam-Christ parallel is built on the principle of federal representation.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it is written, 'The first man Adam became a living being'; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. — 1 Corinthians 15:45
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's title "last Adam" is one of the most theologically loaded phrases in the New Testament. It identifies Christ as the One who takes up where the first Adam left off — a second covenant head, a new representative, a new humanity. Where the first Adam received life and became a living being, the last Adam goes further: He becomes a life-giving spirit, the source of resurrection life for all who are in Him.

The word "last" is also significant: this is not merely a second attempt at what Adam tried and failed. Christ is the last Adam — the definitive, final, unrepeatable human covenant head. There will be no third. What He accomplished — perfect obedience, atoning death, resurrection — is permanently sufficient. The first Adam plunged humanity into death; the last Adam raises it to a life that death cannot touch. Every element of Reformed soteriology hinges on this comparison: imputation of sin (we were in Adam), imputation of righteousness (we are in Christ), condemnation (in Adam's covenant-breaking), justification (in Christ's covenant-keeping). The Covenant of Works is not merely the dark background of the gospel; it is the grammatical structure within which the gospel makes sense.

verseByVerse.ref: Like Adam They Transgressed the Covenant
verseByVerse.quote: But like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me. — Hosea 6:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
This brief verse is among the most disputed in the covenant theology debate. The ESV rendering "like Adam" (following the Hebrew ke'adam) is the reading that most naturally supports the existence of a formal covenant with Adam in Eden — Israel's covenant-breaking is compared to Adam's, implying that Adam's transgression was itself a covenant violation. Some read "like Adam" as a place name ("at Adam"), but the contextual force is strongest when it refers to the first man: the prophetic charge against Israel is that they are repeating the paradigmatic covenant betrayal of their federal head.

The pastoral weight of the comparison is searching. The covenant with Adam was violated at the moment of its testing; the covenant with Israel was violated repeatedly across centuries of patience and grace. Both violations share the same character: knowing the covenant Lord, receiving His gifts, being called to faithfulness — and turning away. Hosea's prophetic task is to call Israel back to covenant loyalty, offering a future restoration (6:1–3) while indicting the present unfaithfulness. The Adam comparison deepens the indictment: this is not merely political rebellion or moral failure — it is the oldest sin in the human story, the sin of the covenant head, repeated by his children.

3.title: The Covenant of Grace
3.overview:
The covenant of works was broken the moment Adam ate. The justice of God demanded death — immediate, complete, irreversible. And yet the story does not end there. In Genesis 3:15, in the immediate aftermath of the fall, God speaks words to the serpent that contain within them the entire gospel in embryo: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel." This is the protoevangelium — the first gospel, the first promise of redemption — and it is the inauguration of the Covenant of Grace.

The Covenant of Grace is God's sovereign, gracious arrangement by which He promises to be the God of His chosen people, to forgive their sins, to renew their hearts, and to bring them to eternal life — not on the basis of their obedience (the works principle of the first covenant) but on the basis of His grace received through faith. The condition of the Covenant of Grace is faith — not as a meritorious act but as the empty hand that receives what God freely gives. And the mediator of the Covenant of Grace is Christ — the last Adam whose obedience satisfies what the first Adam owed and provides the righteousness the covenant requires.

The Covenant of Grace is one — administered under multiple forms (Adamic promise, Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, new covenant) but always the same covenant in its essence: God graciously binding Himself to a people, through Christ, by faith. This is the great Reformed insight that holds the two Testaments together: the same grace, the same Christ (foreshadowed or revealed), the same faith — one people across all ages, one salvation, one Covenant of Grace.
3.theology:
One Covenant, Multiple Administrations

The Westminster Confession (Chapter 7.5–6) articulates the classic Reformed position: "This covenant was differently administered in the time of the law, and in the time of the gospel: under the law it was administered by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances delivered to the people of the Jews... Under the gospel... the ordinances in which this covenant is dispensed are the preaching of the word, and the administration of the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper." Same covenant, different forms — the difference is one of clarity and fullness, not of substance.

The Condition of Faith

The Covenant of Grace is not unconditional in the sense that nothing is required of its members. Faith is the condition — not as a meritorious work that earns the covenant blessings, but as the divinely given instrument through which those blessings are received. This is why the Covenant of Grace is also called the "covenant of faith" in contrast to the covenant of works. But even the faith that meets the condition is itself a covenant gift: "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God" (Eph 2:8). The covenant of grace gives what it requires.

The Dual Aspect: External and Internal

Reformed covenant theology also recognises that the Covenant of Grace has an external administration (membership in the visible covenant community, marked by the covenant sign) and an internal reality (regeneration, saving faith, and genuine union with Christ). Not all who are in the covenant externally are in it savingly — a reality the New Testament acknowledges (Rom 9:6: "not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel"). This distinction is essential for understanding covenant warnings, apostasy, and the relationship between the visible and invisible church.
3.examples:
Then: The genius of covenant theology as developed by the Westminster Divines was to show that Abraham, David, and the New Testament believer are all saved by the same grace, through the same Christ (foreshadowed or revealed), through the same faith. This is what allows Paul to call Abraham "the father of all who believe" (Rom 4:11) and to treat Galatians 3:6–9 as a demonstration that the Abrahamic covenant is the gospel in advance: "the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, 'In you shall all the nations be blessed.' So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith."

Now: The unity of the Covenant of Grace is the Reformed answer to questions about the status of Old Testament believers (Were they saved? By what means? Were they truly in relationship with God?). They were saved by grace, through faith, in the promised Mediator — the same Mediator whose coming they anticipated and whom they trusted in shadow form. The saints of the Old Testament are not second-class members of a preliminary religion; they are fellow heirs of the same promise, members of the same covenant community, saved by the same blood — applied to them prospectively, to us retrospectively.

verseByVerse.quote: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel. — Genesis 3:15
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the oldest verse in the Bible about Jesus, spoken before any law, any covenant sign, any temple or priesthood. It is spoken to the serpent — not to Adam, not to Eve — because it is a declaration of war, not an invitation. God announces that He will place enmity between the serpent and the woman, between the seed of the serpent and the seed of the woman. At the end of that conflict stands a single figure: "he shall bruise your head" — a decisive, fatal blow — "and you shall bruise his heel" — a painful but non-fatal wound. The cross and the resurrection are in embryo here: the serpent wounds the Son of God, but the Son of God crushes the serpent.

This is the inauguration of the Covenant of Grace, and its content is entirely promissory: God acts, God promises, God will provide. Adam and Eve contribute nothing to this promise — they stand there in their shame and newly sewn fig leaves while God speaks words that will take four thousand years to reach their fulfilment at Golgotha. Every subsequent covenant — Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, new — is an unfolding and enriching of this first promise. The scarlet thread begins here and runs to the last page of Revelation, where the serpent is finally and permanently defeated (Rev 20:10).

verseByVerse.quote: And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, 'In you shall all the nations be blessed.' — Galatians 3:8
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's statement here is extraordinary: the Abrahamic covenant was the gospel preached in advance. Not a preliminary, inferior version of the gospel, not a legal arrangement that would be replaced by something better — but the gospel itself, in its essential content: justification by faith, blessing for all nations, the righteousness of God received through trust in His promise. Abraham believed, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Gen 15:6; Rom 4:3). The principle is identical to New Testament justification.

The phrase "in you shall all the nations be blessed" (Gen 12:3; 22:18) is the global horizon of the Covenant of Grace: from the first moment of its Abrahamic administration, the covenant was not merely for Israel but for "all the nations." The particular election of Abraham and his seed was always in service of the universal blessing. Paul uses this to demolish any notion that the Mosaic law was the real heart of the Abrahamic covenant — the law came 430 years later and cannot nullify a prior covenant (Gal 3:17). The heart of the Abrahamic covenant is the gospel: faith receiving the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you. — Genesis 17:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I will be their God" — this covenant formula, first given to Abraham in its fuller form here, echoes through every subsequent covenant administration and finds its ultimate fulfilment in Revelation 21:3: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God." The Covenant of Grace has one content from beginning to end: God giving Himself to a people as their God. Everything else — the land, the law, the sacrifices, the temple, the kingdom — is the unfolding of that central gift.

The word "everlasting" is significant: this is not a temporary arrangement to be superseded by something better. The new covenant does not replace the Abrahamic covenant; it fulfils it. Circumcision gives way to the Spirit, the land becomes the new creation, the nation becomes the church from every nation — but the covenant formula remains: I will be your God, and you will be my people. Herman Witsius saw in this formula the entire substance of covenant theology: God pledging Himself, in all His fulness, to be the covenant God of His people — and the whole of salvation being the progressive unfolding of what that pledge means.

verseByVerse.quote: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. — Jeremiah 31:33
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah 31:31–34 is the only place in the Old Testament where the phrase "new covenant" appears, and it is quoted at length in Hebrews 8 as the charter of the new covenant age. The newness of the new covenant is not its content (the same covenant formula: "I will be their God") but its mode: what was written on stone tablets will now be written on hearts. The externality of the old covenant administration gives way to the internality of the new — not because the law was wrong but because the Spirit will now do what external law could not: transform from within.

The result is universal knowledge of the Lord within the covenant community: "they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest" (v.34). This is not a promise that every person on earth will know God, but that in the new covenant community, the knowledge of God will be the possession of all its members — no longer mediated through priests and prophets to an often-unbelieving people, but direct, personal, Spirit-given. And the ground of it all: "I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more" (v.34). The new covenant is grounded in complete, final, unrepeatable forgiveness — the forgiveness that the blood of bulls and goats could only foreshadow and that the blood of the new covenant Mediator actually achieves.

4.title: The Covenants in the Old Testament
4.overview:
The Covenant of Grace does not arrive in the Old Testament as a single, fully formed institution. It unfolds progressively, through a series of distinct covenantal administrations, each of which enriches and advances the original promise without replacing it. The Noahic covenant establishes the framework of a preserved creation within which redemption will be accomplished. The Abrahamic covenant names the people through whom the promised seed will come and the scope of blessing (all nations). The Mosaic covenant gives the redeemed people a law to live by and a system of worship that points forward to Christ. The Davidic covenant narrows the promise to a royal line — the Messiah will be David's son — and defines the shape of the coming kingdom. Each covenant is a new chapter in the same story, a new unfolding of the same promise, a further illumination of the same Saviour.

This progressive character of the covenants is what gives the Old Testament its dramatic texture: it is not a static body of law or a random collection of stories, but a narrative moving toward a goal — the fulfilment of all the covenants in the One whom they foreshadow. Jesus said: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfil them" (Matt 5:17). Every covenant, every sacrifice, every king, every temple is a promise that Christ redeems. To read the Old Testament through the lens of covenant is to read it as it was designed to be read: as a story that has an ending, and whose ending is Christ.
4.theology:
The Noahic Covenant

The Noahic covenant (Gen 9:8–17) is the broadest and most universal of the biblical covenants, made not only with Noah and his family but with "every living creature" and with "the earth itself." Its content is a promise of preservation — God will not again destroy all life with a flood — and its sign is the rainbow. Reformed theology has understood this as a common grace covenant: God's commitment to maintain the conditions of creation (seasons, day and night — Gen 8:22) within which the work of redemption will be accomplished. It does not save; it sustains the world in which salvation will be worked out.

The Mosaic Covenant and the Law

The Mosaic covenant is the most complex and the most debated. The Reformed tradition has understood it as an administration of the Covenant of Grace — the covenant God made with redeemed Israel at Sinai, giving them His law as the pattern of covenant life. The law does not save (it was never intended to); it defines the shape of the life of the redeemed. But the Mosaic covenant also has what Reformed theologians call a "works element": the conditional blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28–30, which mirror the works principle of the original covenant of works. Paul addresses this complexity in Galatians 3–4, distinguishing the law's role as tutor (Gal 3:24) from the promise, which was always primary.

The Davidic Covenant

The Davidic covenant (2 Sam 7:12–16) narrows the promise of the Covenant of Grace to a specific royal line: the Messiah will be David's son. "I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever" — a promise that no merely human king could fulfill, and that points inescapably beyond David's biological descendants to one who will reign eternally. The psalms of ascent, the royal psalms, and the prophetic promises of a coming Davidic king (Isa 9:6–7; 11:1–5; Jer 23:5–6; Ezek 34:23–24) are all expansions of this covenant. The angel Gabriel's announcement to Mary (Luke 1:32–33) is its fulfilment: "the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever."
4.examples:
Then: The progressive revelation of the covenants is what gives the Old Testament its inner coherence and its forward movement. The prophets could call Israel back to covenant faithfulness, could pronounce covenant curses (Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Jeremiah), and could promise covenant renewal (Isaiah 40–66, Ezekiel 36–37, Jeremiah 31) because the covenant framework was the assumed context of all their preaching. Without understanding the covenants, the prophets become moralists; with it, they become preachers of a coming redemption.

Now: One of the most practical benefits of covenant theology is that it teaches Christians how to read the Old Testament. The ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, temple) is fulfilled in Christ and no longer binding as ceremony — but it is still Scripture, still instructive, still illuminating Christ. The moral law (the Ten Commandments as the summary of covenant obligations) retains its binding force, not as a means of salvation but as the pattern of covenant life for the redeemed. The civil law of Israel is expired with the theocratic nation but teaches principles of justice still applicable. Covenant theology provides the hermeneutical key for navigating these distinctions.

verseByVerse.quote: I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth. — Genesis 9:11
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Noahic covenant is distinctive in several ways: it is the only biblical covenant made explicitly with the whole creation, not just with a people; it is entirely unconditional (God promises without requiring anything of Noah in return); and it is marked by a natural sign — the rainbow — rather than a ritual one. Its content is preservation, not salvation: God commits to sustaining the world so that His redemptive purposes can be worked out within it.

The theological significance of this covenant is considerable: it means that the created order is not a temporary stage to be discarded but a sustained gift, maintained by God's faithfulness for the duration of the redemptive age. It is the basis for what the Reformed tradition calls "common grace" — God's good gifts to all people, regardless of their standing before Him, which preserve human civilization and make life in a fallen world bearable. Peter uses the flood narrative as a type of baptism (1 Pet 3:20–21) and as an analogy for the final judgment (2 Pet 3:5–7) — showing that the Noahic covenant points beyond itself to a final preservation and a final judgment more comprehensive than the flood.

verseByVerse.ref: The Abrahamic Covenant — A People for All Nations
verseByVerse.quote: Now the LORD said to Abram, 'Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you. And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing... and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.' — Genesis 12:1–3
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Abrahamic covenant is the pivot of Old Testament redemptive history. Everything before it — the creation, the fall, the Noahic preservation — has been the preparation. Everything after it — the exodus, the law, the kingdom, the exile, the return — is the unfolding. God calls one man out of paganism, from Ur of the Chaldeans, and through him promises to bless the whole world. The particular is in service of the universal from the very beginning.

The structure of the covenant is entirely one-sided: God commands, God promises, God will provide. The land, the nation, the blessing, the great name — all are God's gifts, not Abram's achievements. This unilateral structure is confirmed in Genesis 15, when God alone passes between the cut animals in the form of a smoking pot and flaming torch — binding Himself by oath to fulfil the promise, regardless of Abram's faithfulness or failure. Geerhardus Vos saw in this ceremony the key to the entire Abrahamic covenant: God is the guarantor, and His faithfulness, not Abraham's, is the covenant's foundation. Paul develops this at length in Romans 4 and Galatians 3–4: the Abrahamic covenant is the charter of justification by faith, and its global horizon is the charter of the Gentile mission.

verseByVerse.ref: The Mosaic Covenant — Law for the Redeemed
verseByVerse.quote: 'You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself. Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples...' — Exodus 19:4–5
verseByVerse.commentary:
The order of Exodus is decisive for understanding the Mosaic covenant: the exodus comes before Sinai, redemption before law. God does not give Israel the law and say "obey this and I will redeem you." He redeems Israel from Egypt and then gives them the law as the pattern of life for the redeemed. The Mosaic law is not a means of earning salvation; it is the shape of the covenant life of a people already saved by grace.

The preamble of the Ten Commandments confirms this: "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery" (Exod 20:2). The identity statement comes before the commandments — God as Redeemer precedes God as lawgiver. The law flows from the redemption; the redemption does not flow from the law. Sinclair Ferguson's The Whole Christ shows how crucial this order is: legalism begins when we separate law from its proper setting in grace, treating the commandments as a means of gaining favour rather than a response to favour already given. The Mosaic covenant is a Covenant of Grace administered through law, not a covenant of law replacing grace.

verseByVerse.ref: The Davidic Covenant — An Eternal Kingdom
verseByVerse.quote: When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom... And I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. — 2 Samuel 7:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathan's oracle to David is one of the most theologically rich passages in the Old Testament. God takes David's desire to build Him a house (a temple) and turns it around: God will build David a house (a dynasty). The word "house" (bayit) pivots between the two meanings, and the reversal is deliberate — God is the builder, David is the recipient, grace is the operating principle. This is the Covenant of Grace in its royal form.

The promise of an eternal throne is made to David's "offspring" — a word (Hebrew zera', seed) that can be singular or collective, individual or corporate. The immediate reference is Solomon; the ultimate reference, as the prophets progressively make clear (Isa 9:6–7; Jer 23:5–6; Ezek 34:23–24; Zech 9:9), is the Messiah. Acts 2:29–36 quotes Psalm 16 and Psalm 110 to show that David himself knew his greater Son was in view — David wrote as a prophet about the resurrection and enthronement of One who would be both his descendant and his Lord (Ps 110:1). The Davidic covenant is the covenantal foundation of the entire New Testament's Christology: Jesus is the Son of David (Matt 1:1), the eternal King whose throne God has established forever.

5.title: The New Covenant
5.overview:
All the covenants of the Old Testament are arrows pointing forward. The Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, and Davidic covenants are not ends in themselves; they are anticipations, each from a different angle, of a covenant yet to come — one that will be unlike the old in its mode and yet the fulfilment of the old in its substance. That covenant is what Jeremiah calls the "new covenant" (Jer 31:31) — and what Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, called "the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20).

The new covenant is new in three decisive ways. First, it is written on the heart rather than on stone — the Spirit does from within what the law could only demand from without. Second, its membership is marked by genuine knowledge of God: "they shall all know me" — not a community of mixed membership in which believers and unbelievers sit side by side, but a community of those who have been genuinely regenerated and who know God personally. Third, it rests on a completed, unrepeatable forgiveness: "I will remember their sin no more" — not the annual covering of Yom Kippur but the once-for-all removal of sins by the sacrifice of the Son of God.

The new covenant is the Covenant of Grace in its final, fullest, most glorious form. It is not a replacement of the prior covenants but their completion — the "yes and amen" that Christ is to every promise of God (2 Cor 1:20). The church that lives under the new covenant is the most privileged covenant community in all of history: we live on the far side of the cross and the resurrection, in the age of the Spirit, reading Scripture that is illuminated by its fulfilment.
5.theology:
Continuity and Discontinuity

Covenant theology has always insisted on both continuity and discontinuity between the old covenant administrations and the new. Continuity: the same Covenant of Grace, the same Mediator (foreshadowed or revealed), the same saving faith, the same people of God, the same moral law. Discontinuity: the ceremonial law fulfilled and therefore no longer binding as ceremony; the civil law of Israel expired with the theocratic nation; the covenant sign changed from circumcision to baptism; the covenant community now explicitly includes Gentiles on equal terms with Jews. The newness of the new covenant is real — Hebrews insists on it — but it is the newness of fulfilment, not replacement.

Hebrews and the Better Covenant

The letter to the Hebrews is the New Testament's most extended exposition of new covenant theology. The argument is consistently from lesser to greater: a better sacrifice (ch.9–10), a better priesthood (ch.7–8), a better covenant (ch.8), a better hope (7:19), a better country (11:16). The "better" is not a rejection of the old but its transcendence: the old was good, pointing to something better; the better has now arrived, and going back to the shadows would be a tragedy.

The Lord's Supper as Covenant Meal

Jesus's institution of the Lord's Supper on the night of His betrayal is explicitly a new covenant act: "This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20). The Passover, the covenant meal of the old covenant, gives way to the Lord's Supper, the covenant meal of the new. As Passover recalled and participated in the exodus redemption, the Lord's Supper recalls and participates in the cross — the definitive, final, eschatological redemption that all the Passovers foreshadowed.
5.examples:
Then: The early church understood itself as the new covenant community from the beginning. Pentecost was the fulfilment of Joel's prophecy (Acts 2:16–21), itself a new covenant promise of the Spirit poured out on all flesh. The inclusion of Gentiles on equal terms (Acts 10–11; Gal 3:28) was not a surprise addition to the plan but the fulfilment of the Abrahamic promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham's seed (Gal 3:14). The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) debated precisely how the new covenant related to the Mosaic — and concluded that the ceremonial requirements of the Mosaic covenant were not binding on Gentile believers in the new covenant age.

Now: Understanding the new covenant transforms how we understand the church, the sacraments, and the Christian life. The church is not a human organisation with spiritual ambitions; it is the new covenant community, the people of the last days, the assembly of those who have been brought into the covenant that all the previous covenants were preparing for. The Lord's Supper is not a memorial ritual we observe out of tradition; it is the new covenant meal, the feast of the new exodus, the participation in the body and blood of the One whose death inaugurated the covenant. Baptism is not a personal statement of faith; it is the covenant sign of entry into the new covenant community.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt... — Jeremiah 31:31–32
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah announces the new covenant in the darkest hour of the old: Jerusalem is about to fall to Babylon, the temple is about to be destroyed, and exile is imminent. Into this darkness comes a promise of a future covenant — one that will address the root problem that the Mosaic covenant exposed but could not cure: the hardness of the human heart. The old covenant was broken by Israel: "they broke my covenant" (v.32). The new covenant will be one that cannot be broken in the same way, because God will ensure its conditions are met from within.

The "not like" of verse 32 is important: the new covenant is not a mere renewal or refinement of the Mosaic covenant. It is genuinely new in its mode of operation — different in administration even if the same in substance. The writer of Hebrews picks this up with great care (Heb 8:7–13): if the first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no need for a second. The fault was not in the covenant's content (the law was holy, righteous, and good — Rom 7:12) but in the people who could not keep it. The new covenant addresses the people problem by addressing the heart.

verseByVerse.ref: The New Covenant in My Blood
verseByVerse.quote: And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, 'This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.' — Luke 22:20
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks these words in the upper room at the Passover meal, taking the cup of the covenant and identifying it with His own blood — the blood that will be shed within hours. The claim is breathtaking: the new covenant that Jeremiah promised six centuries earlier is being inaugurated tonight, in this room, by this Man, through His death. Jesus is identifying Himself as the Mediator of the new covenant — the One whose sacrifice will accomplish what all the old covenant sacrifices could only point to.

The word "poured out" echoes the language of sacrifice — blood poured out at the base of the altar (Lev 4:7). But this pouring out is not at an altar in the temple; it is on a cross outside Jerusalem. And it does not merely cover sin temporarily; it removes it permanently. Every time the Lord's Supper is celebrated, it is a new covenant act: the community of the new covenant gathering around the covenant meal, proclaiming the Lord's death until He comes (1 Cor 11:26), and renewing their covenant participation in the One whose blood is their cleansing, their reconciliation, and the ground of their access to God.

verseByVerse.ref: A Better Covenant on Better Promises
verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises. — Hebrews 8:6
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word "better" in Hebrews is comparative — better than what? Better than the old covenant administration, not better than nothing. The old covenant was good; the new is better. The old pointed to the true; the new is the true. The old had a human high priest who died and had to be replaced; the new has an eternal High Priest who lives forever to intercede. The old had sacrifices that had to be repeated daily and annually; the new has a once-for-all sacrifice that perfects for all time those who are being sanctified (Heb 10:14).

"Better promises" — the promises of the new covenant (Jer 31:31–34) are better not because the old promises were false but because they are the fulfilment of what the old promised. The promise of the land becomes the promise of a new creation; the promise of a nation becomes the promise of people from every nation; the promise of a king becomes the promise of the eternal King; the promise of forgiveness through sacrifice becomes the reality of forgiveness through the once-for-all sacrifice of the Son. Every "better" in Hebrews is the sound of a promise that has found its "yes" in Christ (2 Cor 1:20).

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to them, 'Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.' — Acts 2:38–39
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's Pentecost sermon is a new covenant sermon: the Spirit poured out on the crowd is the fulfilment of Joel's prophecy (Acts 2:16–21), itself a new covenant promise. The gift of the Spirit is the defining mark of new covenant membership — not circumcision, not Torah observance, not ethnic descent, but the Spirit received by those who repent and trust in the risen Christ.

The scope of the promise is as wide as the Abrahamic covenant: "for you and for your children and for all who are far off" — the household, the next generation, and the Gentiles at the ends of the earth. The Abrahamic promise that all nations would be blessed is now being fulfilled as the Spirit falls on Jewish pilgrims from every nation under heaven (Acts 2:5–11) and will fall on Gentiles at Cornelius's house (Acts 10:44–48). The new covenant community is larger than Israel, older than Pentecost (rooted in the eternal covenant of redemption), and will not be complete until the last person the Father has given to the Son has heard the gospel and been sealed with the promised Spirit.

6.title: Covenant Theology and Baptism
6.overview:
Of all the practical implications of covenant theology, none has generated more debate within the Reformed family than the question of baptism. The debate is not about whether baptism matters (all parties agree it does) or whether faith is required for salvation (all agree it is). The debate is about the relationship between the covenant sign and covenant membership, and specifically whether the children of believers should receive the covenant sign of entry into the new covenant community.

The paedobaptist (infant baptism) position, held by the majority of the historic Reformed tradition (Westminster, Heidelberg, Belgic Confessions), argues from the unity and continuity of the Covenant of Grace. If there is one Covenant of Grace from Abraham to the new covenant, and if the children of believers were included in the covenant community under the Abrahamic administration (receiving circumcision as the covenant sign on the eighth day), then the children of believers are included in the new covenant community and should receive its covenant sign — baptism — in the same way. The sign has changed; the principle of household inclusion has not.

The credobaptist (believer's baptism) position, held by Reformed Baptists and others, argues from the newness of the new covenant. If the new covenant community is exclusively a community of the regenerate — those who truly know the Lord (Jer 31:34) — then the covenant sign should be administered only to those who give credible evidence of regeneration, i.e., professing believers. The newness of the new covenant means that the household principle of the Abrahamic administration no longer applies in the same way.

Both positions are serious, biblical, and held by godly Reformed Christians. This unit presents both cases fairly, drawing out the covenant-theological arguments on each side.
6.theology:
The Paedobaptist Case

The paedobaptist argument rests on three pillars: (1) The unity of the Covenant of Grace — one covenant from Genesis 3:15 to the consummation, administered differently but never broken or replaced. (2) The inclusion of children — in the Abrahamic covenant (Gen 17), children of believers were covenant members and received the covenant sign (circumcision); the New Testament nowhere explicitly excludes children from the new covenant community. (3) The parallel between circumcision and baptism — Colossians 2:11–12 connects circumcision and baptism in ways that suggest they are corresponding covenant signs, one for the old administration, one for the new.

The Credobaptist Case

The credobaptist argument also rests on three pillars: (1) The newness of the new covenant — Jeremiah 31:34 says all members of the new covenant will know the Lord; the new covenant community is, by definition, a community of the regenerate. (2) The pattern of baptism in the New Testament — every instance of baptism in Acts follows repentance and faith; there is no clear instance of infant baptism in the New Testament. (3) The sign should match the reality — baptism signifies union with Christ in death and resurrection (Rom 6:3–5), which is a reality only the regenerate possess; giving the sign to those who may not possess the reality risks confusion.

What Both Sides Share

Both paedobaptists and credobaptists within the Reformed tradition agree on the following: baptism is a covenant sign, not a means of regeneration; faith is required for salvation; the children of believers are in a special relationship to the covenant community and should be raised in the faith; and the church must carefully discern genuine faith in those who come to full communion. The disagreement is about the precise nature of new covenant membership and the proper subjects of the covenant sign — a genuine disagreement, but one that should be held with charity between brothers and sisters in Christ.
6.examples:
Then: The paedobaptist position was the consensus of the magisterial Reformers (Luther, Calvin, Zwingli, Bucer) and the confessional Reformed tradition (Westminster, Heidelberg, Belgic). The credobaptist position was held by the Anabaptists in the sixteenth century and was developed with rigorous Reformed covenantal arguments by the London Baptist Confession of 1689, which adapted the Westminster Confession while substituting a credobaptist doctrine of the church and sacraments. The Second London Confession represents the maturity of Reformed Baptist covenant theology — a serious attempt to hold Reformed doctrine while arguing from the newness of the new covenant for believer's baptism only.

Now: The debate between paedobaptists and credobaptists continues among Reformed Christians, and it is a debate worth having carefully and charitably. What covenant theology rules out is the common evangelical view of baptism as merely a personal testimony or a public declaration of an individual's decision — as if baptism were primarily about us rather than about God's covenant claim on us. Both Reformed paedobaptists and Reformed credobaptists understand baptism as a covenant act, administered in the name of the Trinity, which makes a claim and creates an obligation. The disagreement is about who may receive it; the agreement is about what it means.

verseByVerse.quote: This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised... So shall my covenant be in your flesh an everlasting covenant. — Genesis 17:10, 13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham in Genesis 17 — the mark cut into the flesh that signified membership in the covenant community. Three things are notable: (1) It was given to the household, not only to Abraham himself — "every male among you," including those born in the house and those bought with money (v.12), i.e., not only biological descendants but the whole household. (2) It was given to infants — on the eighth day (v.12), before the child could express faith or understanding. (3) It signified a reality the recipient did not yet possess — not all who were circumcised were inwardly circumcised (Rom 2:28–29; 9:6).

The paedobaptist draws the direct parallel: baptism is the new covenant sign corresponding to circumcision (Col 2:11–12); what circumcision was for the old covenant community, baptism is for the new. The household principle that governed the administration of circumcision carries over: the children of believers, as members of the covenant household, receive the covenant sign. The credobaptist responds: the parallel holds for what the signs signify, but the new covenant's more complete and explicit emphasis on the regenerate nature of the community means the administration of the sign must be restricted to those who give evidence of the inward reality.

verseByVerse.quote: In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism... — Colossians 2:11–12
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's connection of circumcision and baptism in this passage is the exegetical centre of the paedobaptist-credobaptist debate. He describes the Colossians as having received a circumcision "made without hands" — a spiritual circumcision, the regenerating work of the Spirit on the heart. And he connects this to baptism: "having been buried with him in baptism." The natural reading is that circumcision and baptism are parallel covenant signs, one the mark of the old covenant, the other the mark of the new.

For the paedobaptist, this parallel means that baptism inherits the covenantal function of circumcision: as circumcision marked entry into the old covenant community (including household infants), baptism marks entry into the new covenant community. For the credobaptist, the parallel is real but the administration differs: the "circumcision made without hands" Paul describes is a spiritual reality (regeneration) that precedes and grounds the baptism — suggesting that baptism should follow evidence of that spiritual reality, i.e., professing faith. Both readings are exegetically possible; the debate turns on the weight given to the continuity or discontinuity between the covenantal administrations.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family. — Acts 16:33
verseByVerse.commentary:
The baptism of the Philippian jailer and "all his family" is one of several household baptisms in Acts (see also Cornelius in Acts 10:48, Lydia in 16:15, Crispus in 18:8, Stephanas in 1 Cor 1:16). The paedobaptist argument notes that these households are baptized without any explicit statement that every individual member first made a profession of faith — and that in households of the ancient world, infants and young children would typically be included in "all his family." The household principle, they argue, is continuous with the Abrahamic household principle: the covenant sign goes to the household of the believer.

The credobaptist responds that Acts 16:34 says the jailer "rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God" — suggesting that faith preceded baptism for the members of the household. The word "household" (oikos) may refer to older members who themselves believed. Neither side can prove from this text alone that infants were or were not included; the text is genuinely ambiguous. What it does show is that the New Testament pattern of evangelism and baptism was household-shaped — conversion of the head of the household resulted in the baptism of the whole household — which sits more naturally with the paedobaptist reading of covenant inclusion than with an individualist pattern of decision and baptism.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. — Romans 6:3–4
verseByVerse.commentary:
Romans 6 is the New Testament's richest statement of what baptism signifies: union with Christ in His death and resurrection. The baptized person has been identified with the dying Christ (buried with Him) and with the risen Christ (raised to walk in newness of life). This is the full reality that the sign of baptism points to — and it is a reality that only the genuinely regenerate possess. This text is the credobaptist's strongest argument: if baptism signifies this kind of union with Christ, it should be administered only to those in whom this union is evidenced by genuine faith.

The paedobaptist does not deny the weight of this argument but responds that the covenant sign has always pointed to a reality that the recipient may or may not yet possess savingly. Circumcision signified the circumcision of the heart (Deut 10:16; 30:6; Jer 4:4) — a reality not all who were circumcised possessed. Giving the sign to the household of the believer does not imply that every member is regenerate; it places them within the covenant community, under the covenant obligations and covenant promises, with the earnest prayer and expectation that the Spirit will make the sign a reality. The sign is a pledge — God's pledge to the child through the parents — not a certificate of regeneration. Both positions call for pastoral care, catechism, and eventual personal profession of faith; they differ on when the sign is administered.
